knowledge: Claude can turn messy inputs such as interview notes, emails, survey comments and tickets into a structured list of requirements, grouped by theme, with gaps and conflicts flagged.
Claude works only from what you give it: context about the team, volumes, pain points and constraints turns a generic answer into a useful analysis.
Claude can add plausible requirements or details that nobody actually stated, so every requirement should trace back to a source you can check.
Good first use cases are frequent, text-heavy and easy for a person to check before the output is used.
Use cases that need live data moving between systems, automation at scale or custom integrations are technical builds: Associates define the need and escalate them to Claude Developers or Architects.
skills: Ask Claude to extract requirements, cite where each one came from, and list open questions for stakeholders.
Turn vague requirements ("fast", "easy to use") into measurable questions to confirm with stakeholders.
Score candidate use cases on frequency, time spent, risk and ease of review, then start with a low-risk one.
Write a short brief of the business need and success criteria before handing technical work to a Developer or Architect.
examLens: A "best first step" in a requirements question is usually giving Claude real context or tracing a claim to its source, not accepting the output.
If the use case needs systems connected or automated at scale, the answer is to define requirements and escalate, not to build it yourself.
Prefer a frequent, low-risk, easily checked task as a starting point over the most visible high-stakes one.
traps: Treating a requirement Claude added as fact because it sounds like best practice.
Asking a generic question ("Is AI good for customer service?") and judging Claude by the generic answer.
Promising a client a technical integration you are not positioned to build.

knowledge: Web search suits simple, current questions and every web-search answer includes citations; Research runs many searches that build on each other and produces an in-depth report with citations.
Research takes longer and uses your usage allowance faster than normal chat, so save it for questions that need many sources.
Cited sources still need checking: the original page may hold context that Claude’s summary left out.
For process optimization Claude needs the current state: the steps, owners, times, handoffs and pain points.
Claude cannot see constraints you don’t tell it about, such as a compliance check or a contractual step, so owners must review any proposed cut.
Large plans work better broken into stages you review one at a time, with the plan’s assumptions listed openly.

Pilot a proposed change with a small group and compare it with a measured baseline.
examLens: Before leadership sees a research report, check the key figures against their cited sources.
A proposed process change is checked with the process owners and piloted before it is rolled out.
A plan with dates is only as good as the constraints you gave Claude; ask it to state its assumptions.
traps: Treating a citation as proof without opening it.
Removing a step Claude calls redundant when it exists for compliance or a contract.
Asking for a whole project or semester plan in one prompt and accepting it as is.

knowledge: An artifact is something Claude makes that you would put in front of someone, such as a document, deck, dashboard or small interactive tool; it opens beside the chat and can be edited, revisited and shared.
With code execution and file creation turned on, Claude can create Excel files with working formulas, Word, PowerPoint and PDF files, and analyse uploaded data with charts.
Asking for several options with trade-offs against your criteria gives better designs than asking for "the best" one.
Iteration works best with specific feedback and one change at a time, retested on the same real inputs.
Generated files and calculations still need review: check formulas and spot-check numbers before decisions rest on them.
A prototype that proves value is the handoff point: running it automatically for everyone or connecting it to other systems is Developer or Architect work.

examLens: Prototype in an artifact, test with real users, then iterate; don’t wait for IT to start exploring.
When a prototype must scale or connect to company systems, escalate it with evidence.
Specific feedback beats starting over with the same prompt or switching models first.
traps: Trusting a spreadsheet because Claude "ran the calculation".

Connectors let Claude read data and take actions in apps such as Google Drive or Gmail; on Team and Enterprise an Owner must enable a connector first, and each person still signs in with their own account.

knowledge: Claude’s value: faster drafting, summarizing, analysis and research, consistent first drafts, and time freed for work that needs judgement.
Claude can produce convincing but incorrect content, including invented quotes or figures, so it is not a single source of truth.
Claude can also misstate its own capabilities, for example claiming it sent an email; it has no access to tools that are not connected.
Claude only knows what is in the conversation, the project knowledge or connected tools, and connected tools follow each person’s own permissions.
Credible business cases rest on measured pilot results and stated limits, not vendor claims or hand-picked demos.
The person who sends or acts on the output stays responsible for it.

examLens: The best stakeholder message is balanced: real gains plus the checks that stay in place.
Overpromising (headcount cuts, "always accurate") is always a distractor.
After an incident, explain and strengthen review rather than abandon Claude or blame it.
traps: Saying a newer or larger model removes the need to check facts.

Building a case on the best outputs from a demo.

knowledge: Anthropic’s Usage Policy applies to everyone who uses Claude. It has universal usage standards, requirements for high-risk use cases, and additional use-case guidelines.
Prohibited uses include fraud and predatory practices, deceptive campaigns, disinformation, surveillance, and compromising people’s privacy, among others.

High-risk uses such as legal, medical, financial, insurance, housing, employment and education decisions need a qualified person who reviews the AI output before it is acted on, and disclosure to the affected person that AI was used.
Internal drafting, research and summaries that are not the final recommendation, and business operations not deciding about a specific person, fall outside the high-risk category.
Chatbots that face consumers must tell users they are talking to AI.
Low-stakes tasks such as brainstorming, formatting and internal drafts are good fits with normal review.
skills: Sort a request into low-stakes, high-risk or not allowed.
Redesign a high-risk request so Claude assists and a qualified person decides.
Offer a legitimate alternative when declining an inappropriate request.
Recognize when a customer-facing build needs AI disclosure and a Developer or Architect.
examLens: Decisions about a specific person’s job, loan, housing, grades or health: human in the loop and disclosure, never full automation.
Fake reviews, impersonation and covert profiling are inappropriate whatever the business reason.
The right answer rarely bans Claude outright; it scopes Claude to a safe role.
traps: Fully automating a decision about people because the model seems accurate.
Hiding that a chatbot is AI to improve engagement.
Treating every task touching a regulated industry as high-risk, even internal research.

knowledge: On commercial products such as Team and Enterprise, Anthropic by default does not train on your inputs and outputs; on consumer plans (Free, Pro, Max) chats may be used for training if the user allows it in the model-improvement setting.
Incognito chats aren’t saved to history or memory and aren’t used for training, but they are still kept for a period, and on Team and Enterprise they are included in organization data exports.
Telling Claude to "forget" or "not retain" data does not satisfy a policy control; the control is what you share in the first place.
Connectors inherit your permissions: Claude can reach what you can reach in that service, no more, and can take actions there.
Data minimization: share only the fields the task needs; remove, mask or aggregate identifiers; use placeholders and fill real details in afterwards.
Client contracts and regulations can restrict third-party processing no matter how secure the tool is.

knowledge: Claude can reflect biases from its training or from the inputs you give it, so outputs about people need checking for unfair patterns.
Accountability stays with people: whoever sends or acts on an output owns it, not the AI.
Transparency means telling people when AI shaped content or decisions that affect them, as policy requires, and never presenting AI output deceptively.
Over-reliance erodes skills and judgement; people should be able to explain and check the work they hand in.
Workflow changes affect colleagues, so be open about how roles will change and involve the people affected.
Biased, inaccurate or harmful outputs can be reported with the thumbs-down button or to Anthropic’s user-safety address.
skills: Remove irrelevant personal details from inputs and set job-related criteria before Claude assesses people.
Spot and correct stereotyped or one-sided wording.
Disclose AI use honestly when asked or when policy requires it.
Own and fix an error rather than blame the tool.
examLens: A pattern in outputs that tracks something irrelevant (school, name, age) is a bias signal: fix the inputs and criteria and keep people reviewing.
"The AI did it" is never an acceptable answer to an error.
Honest disclosure beats hiding AI use, even when it is awkward.
traps: Assuming AI is neutral because it has no opinions.
Quietly reusing a biased output after editing a few words.
Rolling out workflow changes without telling the people whose work changes.
